title: Vaping While You Smoke May Nearly Triple Your Risk of Early-Onset Lung Cancer, Study Finds
excerpt: An Ohio State study of more than 3,000 young adults found that those who both vaped and smoked had 2.8 times the lung cancer risk of smokers who never vaped — a finding with sharp relevance for diaspora youth abroad
body:
India took a drastic step in 2019, banning the manufacture, sale, and import of electronic cigarettes under the Prohibition of Electronic Cigarettes Act. The government cited "an epidemic of e-cigarettes" among young people. But for millions of Indians living in the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia — where vaping is legal, widely available, and marketed as a safer alternative to smoking — the landscape is starkly different.

Now, a study from The Ohio State University's Comprehensive Cancer Center adds a harrowing data point: young adults under 50 who both vape and smoke cigarettes face nearly three times the lung cancer risk of those who only smoke. The research, published in *Frontiers in Oncology*, is among the first to quantify the combined effect in humans.

The Numbers Are Difficult to Ignore

Researchers compared the smoking and vaping habits of 256 young adults diagnosed with pathologically confirmed lung cancer to 2,921 cancer-free controls matched by age, sex, race, and location. The results were striking:

  • Those who **only smoked** had an odds ratio of 5.0 for lung cancer compared to non-smokers and non-vapers
  • Those who **both vaped and smoked** had an odds ratio of 13.8 — a 2.8-fold increase over smoking alone
  • For **pulmonary adenocarcinoma** — the most common subtype, accounting for 72% of early-onset tumors — the gap was even wider: an odds ratio of 14.8 for dual users versus 4.0 for smokers only, a 3.7-fold multiplier

> "The government cited "an epidemic of e-cigarettes" among young people."

"Our findings suggest that compared to smoking alone, vaping and smoking together accelerate lung cancer risk among young people," the authors wrote, calling for urgent public health attention to dual use.

Why the Combination Is More Dangerous

The biological mechanism points to synergistic damage. Nicotine inhaled from e-cigarette aerosol can be converted in the body into nitrosamines — potent carcinogens that are also present in cigarette smoke. When both delivery systems are used, the DNA repair machinery in lung and bladder cells faces a double assault: the same types of mutations from two different directions, with the body's ability to fix the damage overwhelmed.

Earlier animal studies from New York University lend support. Mice exposed to e-cigarette vapour for a period equivalent to three to six years of human vaping developed lung adenocarcinomas at a rate of 22.5%, compared to 2.6% in controls. The carcinogenic pathway — nicotine to nitrosamines to DNA adducts — mirrors what cigarette smoke does, but through a different delivery vehicle.

The Diaspora Dimension

For the Indian diaspora, this research carries particular weight. While India's vaping ban means young people at home have limited legal access to e-cigarettes, the picture is reversed abroad. In the United States, more than 2.5 million high school students used e-cigarettes in 2024, according to the CDC. Among South Asian American youth, who may also smoke hookah socially at lounges and gatherings, dual exposure is a real concern.

The study did not break down results by ethnicity, but the risk mechanism is universal: anyone inhaling both vapour and smoke is compounding their carcinogenic exposure.

There is also a generational irony at play. Many South Asian parents who emigrated from India brought with them the cultural habit of occasional smoking — beedis, cigarettes, or hookah. Their children, raised abroad, adopted vaping as what seemed like a modern, less harmful alternative. If both habits coexist in a household or a social circle, the combined risk may be silently accumulating.

A Broader Pattern

Nature Medicine published a commentary in June 2026 warning that real-world evidence from a nationwide cohort suggests e-cigarette use after smoking cessation may attenuate the benefits of quitting in reducing lung cancer risk and mortality. The editorial called for "more studies urgently" to inform evidence-based guidance.

India's ban, controversial at the time for seeming paternalistic, may prove prescient. For NRIs living where vaping is ubiquitous, the takeaway from this study is clear: if you vape, don't smoke, and if you smoke, don't vape. The combination appears far more dangerous than either habit alone.

*Sources: Bittoni et al., Frontiers in Oncology (2026); Tang et al., Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (2019); Nature Medicine commentary, June 2026; CDC National Youth Tobacco Survey (2024)*
